newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin stand on privatisations leaves options open.
newsitem.headline: Jospin stand on privatisations leaves options open.

text.p: Prime Minister Lionel Jospin said on Thursday that his government did not favour privatisations unless they were in the national interest -- a caveat that appeared to leave his options open, traders and analysts said.
Stocks in companies involved in privatisations slumped on Jospin's remarks but rebounded shortly afterwards as investors took heart from signs that his opposition was not rock-hard.
Analysts said Jospin's concern about the state of public finances, which he called "serious," might leave the new government reluctant to rule out such rich sources of revenue.

Jospin said he did not want to stop French state firms from striking partnerships with other European companies, a sentiment seen as another sign of flexibility since many European companies insist on partners in the private sector.

"In the absence of a justification based on the national interest, we are not favourable to the privatisation of this shared heritage that the big state enterprises in competitive industries represent," Jospin said in a keynote policy speech.
"Even so, it will be necessary for them to adapt in order to retain our rank among the most developed nations of the world and to get closer to other European partners," he said.

Jospin's stance on privatisations has been eagerly awaited by stockmarket investors, who were anticipating the start of France's biggest ever French privatisation -- the sale of a minority stake in France Telecom this month.

"On privatisations, it is interesting that he makes the distinction between the public service and the public sector. It was a balanced statement. I would not read this as saying France Telecom is not going to be privatised," said JP Morgan economist David Naude.

The change in government also froze the privatisation under way of the state's 58 percent stake in defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF. The previous government had opened the auction and declared two bids receivable.

Thomson-CSF shares initially tumbled more than four percent, but then surged back into positive territory and finished up 0.33 percent after Jospin spoke in favour of the consolidation under way in the defence sector.
"Our (defence) enterprises must consolidate, to restore and increase their competitiveness so they can fully participate in future cooperation projects in Europe," Jospin said.

"Europe is important for our defence. The government hopes to instill a new dynamism in the cooperation that will develop in this area. It is thus urgent to adopt a new and more coherent policy for the defence industries," he said.

One stock trader said the market perceived Jospin's comments on the need for a common European defence as overriding his stance on privatisations. "But I don't think there's any way they'll privatise Thomson-CSF," the trader said.
"There are more questions than answers," said deputy Francois d'Aubert of the conservative UDF party, referring to the prospects for France Telecom.
The new government has adopted a clearer position in the transport industry, starting with the appointment of Communist Jean-Claude Gayssot to head the transport ministry.
Gayssot said on June 6 that he did not see himself presiding over privatisations, signalling that flag carrier Air France -- on the conservatives' privatisation list -- would remain in state hands.
